text: Why is Canada's capital Ottawa, and not Toronto or Montreal, the two giant cities right next to it?
For a long time, Canada couldn't decide.
Three years later, it moved to Montreal.
Then, in 1849, an angry mob burned Montreal's parliament to the ground.
So the government just started moving. Toronto, then Quebec City, then Toronto, then Quebec again. Every few years, the whole parliament packed its boxes and left.
The problem was that Canada was really two places. English speakers in the west, French speakers in the east. And each side wanted the capital.
And there was a bigger problem. America.
In the War of 1812, American troops had captured Toronto, then called York, and burned its parliament.
Toronto, Kingston and Montreal all sat right on the border, or on the Saint Lawrence, a river an enemy fleet could sail straight up.
But far up the Ottawa River, there was a small lumber town called Bytown.
After the war, the British cut the Rideau Canal through two hundred kilometers of forest, so troops could reach Kingston without passing American guns.
Bytown sat at the canal's northern end, hidden in the woods, and exactly on the river between English and French Canada.
It was renamed Ottawa, and in 1857 the choice went to Queen Victoria. She picked Ottawa.
Not everyone was impressed. One critic called it a sub-arctic lumber village, converted by royal mandate into a political cockpit.
Today, Toronto has almost three million people. Montreal, almost two.
Ottawa has about one. Which is exactly the point. It was chosen to be hard to reach.
